audits.question: Check Old Persian/Elamite/Babylonian royal trilingualism and its administrative limits using an inscription or archive passage; distinguish monumental ideology from the languages of all subjects and daily provisioning.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/persia-achaemenid.md lines 41-48, 54, 57 — line 41 (Old Persian: 'royal inscriptions and elite objects dominate the familiar corpus'; 'not the language of every imperial subject'); line 42 (Elamite: 'extensive Persepolis administrative records'); line 44 (Aramaic row: 'Monumental trilingualism does not exclude a different, widely used administrative medium'); line 47 (Stolper & Tavernier ARTA 2007.001 publishes 'an important counterexample... the first "practical" Old Persian text known', whose readings the entry deliberately does not restate); line 54 (Behistun row: 'Repeats the king's accession/victory claim across scribal traditions'); line 57 ('Choose a work language by transaction and institution, not only by royal ancestry')
audits.entry_claim: Bounded assertion tested: Behistun repeats the king's accession/victory claim across Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian scribal traditions as monumental royal display; Old Persian's attested corpus is dominated by royal inscriptions and is not thereby the language of every imperial subject; monumental trilingualism does not exclude other widely used administrative media, with the Persepolis Fortification records documenting daily provisioning chiefly in Elamite (plus an Aramaic strand); and the Stolper-Tavernier Old Persian administrative tablet (Fort. 1208-101) is a real counterexample to 'Old Persian = display only' that does not by itself demonstrate general practical use.
audits.source_citation: Matthew W. Stolper and Jan Tavernier (2007), 'From the Persepolis Fortification Archive Project, 1: An Old Persian Administrative Tablet from the Persepolis Fortification,' ARTA 2007.001 (Achemenet, June 2007), pp. 1-2 and 5-8 [with Elamite/Aramaic/seal-strand enumeration at pp. 1-2 and the 'practical' text discussion at pp. 6-8]. Retrieved this pass in full; the entry (lines 25, 47) records that this same PDF could not be retrieved in its earlier pass and described the find only from the project's annual report.
audits.source_locator: PDF pp. 1-2: archive composition 'tablets and fragments with texts in Elamite language, in cuneiform script, representing perhaps 15,000-18,000 original documents; tablets and fragments with texts in Aramaic language, in Aramaic script, representing perhaps 700-1,000 original documents; and tablets or tags with seal impressions but no discernible texts... products of three strands of a single information system'; pp. 5-8: 'An Old Persian Tablet... a damaged clay tablet with Old Persian cuneiform script representing a text in Old Persian language, an administrative record... In the reign of Darius I, at least one Persian in Persia wrote Persian language in Persian script'; 'Prevailing characterizations of Old Persian language and script do not account for the existence of this solitary Old Persian tablet'; 'What is extraordinary is to find Old Persian in an administrative record, a "practical" text.'
audits.source_excerpt: What is extraordinary is to find Old Persian in an administrative record, a 'practical' text. It may not demonstrate general use of Old Persian, but even as an isolate it indicates wider use than previously supposed.
audits.retrieval_method: Direct download of the open-access Achemenet PDF (HTTP 200, application/pdf, 1,242,395 bytes) with curl; text extracted with pdftotext (pages 1-3 and full document) and key sentences located by grep in the worker scratch tree. Language inspected: English (authors' published English article); no translation mediator; raw PDF and extraction kept only in reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-09/ (ARTA-2007.001-Stolper-Tavernier.pdf, arta-full.txt).
audits.basis: The archive-composition passage shows daily records ran in Elamite cuneiform (~15,000-18,000 documents) with an Aramaic strand (~700-1,000) and sealed non-textual tags, i.e. work language chosen by transaction and institution, not by royal trilingual display. The unique Old Persian tablet Fort. 1208-101, dated to Darius I's reign by context, is 'an administrative record' whose existence 'contravenes stated expectations' — confirming the entry's counterexample while ARTA itself cautions the isolate 'may not demonstrate general use', so it neither makes Old Persian the language of all subjects nor erases the monumental/practical division the entry draws.
audits.coupling_implication: Supports the entry's language-royal myth-administration coupling as layered, not fused: monumental Behistun trilingualism is the dynasty's authorized display voice; archive provisioning and correspondence run in Elamite/Aramaic by institution; the single Old Persian practical tablet widens, without collapsing, that boundary. A worldbuilding system should keep royal voice, authorized translation, and archival record as separable fields, exactly as entry line 61 requires.
audits.limits: Verdict is corpus-level, not exhaustive: ARTA itself stresses the Old Persian tablet is unique (so far), so 'not the language of every imperial subject' is supported structurally (who wrote what, in which archive), not by a census of speech. The tablet's own Old Persian text readings were not restated by this worker beyond ARTA's description, matching the entry's deliberate restraint at line 47. Hallock 1969 pp. 6, 42-43 (pirradaziš, halmi) were not re-downloaded this pass — the Oriental Institute's OIP-92 page returned no PDF href in this pass's probe — so that wording stands on the entry's earlier inspection, not a fresh retrieval. Corroboration rows use livius.org transcriptions/translations as access aids only; they are not editions of record and neither livius page is the Godley Loeb. No restricted works were redistributed; no claim about subject populations' spoken languages is made from archive languages.

corroborations.label: corroboration_1_behistun_db70
corroborations.source_citation: Darius I, Behistun (DB) column iv lines 87-92 = DB §70, Old Persian transliteration with adapted King/Thompson English translation, Livius.org, 'Behistun T 42' (access aid cited by entry line 60).
corroborations.source_locator: Livius 'Behistun T 42', translation of column iv lines 87-92 (DB §70)
corroborations.source_excerpt: it was in Aryan script, and it was composed on clay tablets and on parchment. ... And it was inscribed and was read off before me. Afterwards this inscription I sent off everywhere among the provinces.
corroborations.relevance: Retrieved full transliteration + translation of the entry's cited passage: supports the mediated-authority claim (production, reading before the king, circulation to the provinces) as royal ideology rather than evidence of universal literacy or subject-language usage.

corroborations.label: corroboration_2_dna_monumental_ideology
corroborations.source_citation: Darius I, DNa (Naqsh-e Rustam), Old Persian transliteration with English translation, Livius.org, 'DNa' (access aid cited by entry line 24).
corroborations.source_locator: Livius 'DNa', opening creation formula and tribute passage
corroborations.source_excerpt: A great god is Ahuramazda, who created this earth, who created yonder sky, who created man, who created happiness for man, who made Darius king, one king of many, one lord of many.

audits.question: Check the winged-figure/Faravahar identification problem against scholarly wording: separate contemporary caption, proposed Ahuramazda/fravashi/xvarenah identification and modern ethical feather/ring diagrams.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/persia-achaemenid.md lines 74-84 — line 79 ('This is Ahuramazda': 'Influential interpretation, not a universally accepted identification... proximity to an Ahuramazda inscription is not a direct caption'); line 80 ('This is royal glory,' farr/xvarənah: 'important scholarly alternative, associated with the debate represented by Shahbazi and Boyce'); line 81 ('fravaši / guardian spirit': 'Familiar later identification, disputed as an Achaemenid reading'); lines 82-83 (wing layers = good thoughts/words/deeds and ring = covenant/loyalty: 'Modern didactic interpretation' / 'Modern devotional reading, not ancient exegesis', quoting a Zoroastrian essay's 'ring of covenant, loyalty and faithfulness', with 'no ancient Achaemenid text glosses these elements, and Boyce (2000) records no certain ancient representation of the fravašis'); line 84 ('Faravahar' is 'a useful modern lookup label, not an attested Achaemenid caption')
audits.entry_claim: Bounded assertion tested: no attested Achaemenid caption names the winged figure/disk ('Faravahar' is a modern lookup label); its ancient referent is contested between a proposed Ahuramazda identification (influential but not universally accepted), a royal-glory/xvarənah reading (important scholarly alternative), and a fravaši/guardian-spirit reading (familiar later identification, disputed as Achaemenid), with Boyce recording no certain ancient plastic representation of the fravašis and modern Zoroastrians still generally reading the symbol as a fravaši; the wing-layer/feather and ring meanings circulated in modern devotional essays are reception, not ancient exegesis.
audits.source_citation: Mary Boyce (2000), 'Fravaši,' Encyclopaedia Iranica X/2: 195-199 (online publication dated 15 December 2000, last updated 31 January 2012), final section. Inspected via an Internet Archive snapshot of the published article text, per the entry's own documented access route (line 22).
audits.source_locator: Article's final paragraphs (print pp. 198-199): 'There is no certain plastic representation of the fravaši s.' — immediately followed by the Moulton sentence, the Zoroastrian-reception clause, and the xvarənah sentence with references to Boyce, Zoroastrianism II p. 103 n. 82 and Boyce and Grenet III p. 104 nn. 197-98.
audits.source_excerpt: Moulton accordingly (p. 260), rejecting the then prevailing Western interpretation of the Achaemenid winged symbol as that of Ahura Mazdā, identified it as the king's fravaši, and it is still generally regarded as a fravaši symbol by Zoroastrians.
audits.retrieval_method: Live Encyclopaedia Iranica under automated access refused this pass (HTTP 403 on iranicaonline.org/articles/faravahar, 2026-10-17); fetched Internet Archive snapshot id 20261009104155 of iranicaonline.org/articles/fravasi-/ via curl (HTTP 200, 400,628 bytes HTML), entity-unescaped and tag-stripped in the worker scratch tree, and located the three key sentences verbatim by string search. Language inspected: English; the archived page is the published article text with its print attribution footer (Vol. X, Fasc. 2, pp. 195-199); snapshot HTML kept only at reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-09/boyce-fravasi-snapshot.html.
audits.basis: The retrieved article states verbatim that 'There is no certain plastic representation of the fravašis', reports Moulton's identification of the Achaemenid winged symbol as the king's fravaši made against 'the then prevailing Western interpretation... that of Ahura Mazdā' (showing the Ahuramazda reading was a prevailing interpretation, i.e. influential, not an ancient caption), records that it is 'still generally regarded as a fravaši symbol by Zoroastrians' (modern reception, exactly as entry line 84 states), and notes 'Strong arguments... for its representing xᵛarənah' (the scholarly alternative). This matches every element of the entry's calibration that the identifications are competing named hypotheses without an ancient caption.
audits.coupling_implication: Grounds the entry's form→placement→patron→contemporary wording→later interpretation layering: no ancient gloss exists to settle the referent, so a worldbuilding system must carry visible motif, royal use, and later religious/national readings as separate fields; modern devotional feather/ring diagrams can be modeled as in-world reception history (entry line 85) but not printed as ancient Achaemenid exegesis.
audits.limits: Scope is partial because two cited substrata were not independently retrieved this pass: (1) Shahbazi 1974, 'An Achaemenid Symbol, I' (AMI n.F. 7: 135-144) — no open digital copy located, so his own argumentation remains bibliographic here, and the Ahuramazda reading's status rests on Boyce's retrospective sentence rather than on any retrieved Shahbazi text; (2) the 2008 Zoroastrian community essay quoted at entry line 83 — not found this pass (tenets.zoroastrianism.com/farohar33.html now resolves to a 404 at parsizoroastrianism.com; DuckDuckGo and Bing phrase searches for 'ring of covenant, loyalty and faithfulness' returned no usable result), so that quotation remains the entry author's side, unchecked here. An Iranica 'Faravahar' article by Shahbazi could not be confirmed either live (403) or in archive captures (CDX prefix queries for faravahar*/faravakar* returned no 200 captures). Boyce is 2000 scholarship consulted via a 2026 archive snapshot; the print page attribution (X/2: 195-199) comes from the archived page's own footer. The retrieved sentences support the coexistence of hypotheses and the absence of an ancient fravaši representation; they do not verify any single identification as correct, and this worker makes no such claim.
